prompt.text: On what ground can you say that scandium $(Z=21)$ is a transition element but zinc $(Z=30)$ is not?

flow.text: Scandium has incompletely filled $3 d$ orbitals in its ground state $\left(3 d^{1}\right)$. So it is regarded as a transition element. Zinc, on the other hand, has completely filled $d$ orbitals $\left(3 d^{10}\right)$ in its ground state as well as in its oxidised state. So it is not regarded as a transition element.

prompt.text: Why do the transition elements exhibit higher enthalpies of atomisation?

flow.text: Transition elements have a large number of unpaired electrons in their atoms. This gives stronger interatomic interaction and hence stronger bonding between atoms. As a result, they have higher enthalpies of atomisation.

prompt.text: Name a transition element which does not exhibit variable oxidation states.

flow.text: Scandium $(Z=21)$ does not exhibit variable oxidation states.

prompt.text: Why is $\mathrm{Cr}^{2+}$ reducing and $\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}$ oxidising when both have $d^{4}$ configuration?

flow.text: $\mathrm{Cr}^{2+}$ is reducing because its configuration changes from $d^{4}$ to $d^{3}$. The latter has a half-filled $t_{2 \mathrm{~g}}$ level (see Unit 5). On the other hand, the change from $\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}$ to $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$ gives the half-filled ( $d^{5}$ ) configuration, which has extra stability.

prompt.text: How would you account for the increasing oxidising power in the series $\mathrm{VO}_{2}{ }^{+}<\mathrm{Cr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{7}{ }^{2-}<\mathrm{MnO}_{4}{ }^{-}$?

flow.text: This is due to the increasing stability of the lower species to which they are reduced.

For the first row transition metals the $E^{\mathrm{o}}$ values are:

| $\boldsymbol{E}^{\circ}$ | V | Cr | Mn | Fe | Co | Ni | Cu |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

Explain the irregularity in the above values.

flow.text: The $E^{\circ}\left(\mathrm{M}^{2+} / \mathrm{M}\right)$ values are not regular. This can be explained by the irregular variation of ionisation enthalpies ( $\Delta_{\mathrm{i}} H_{1}+\Delta_{\mathrm{i}} H_{2}$ ). It can also be explained by the sublimation enthalpies, which are relatively much less for manganese and vanadium.

prompt.text: Why is the $E^{\circ}$ value for the $\mathrm{Mn}^{3+} / \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$ couple much more positive than that for $\mathrm{Cr}^{3+} / \mathrm{Cr}^{2+}$ or $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+} / \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ? Explain.

flow.text: This is mainly because Mn has a much larger third ionisation energy (the required change here is $d^{5}$ to $d^{4}$ ). This also explains why the +3 state of Mn is of little importance.

prompt.text: Calculate the magnetic moment of a divalent ion in aqueous solution if its atomic number is 25.

flow.text: With atomic number 25, the divalent ion in aqueous solution will have $d^{5}$ configuration (five unpaired electrons).

The magnetic moment, $\mu$ is

$$
\mu=\sqrt{5(5+2)}=5.92 \mathrm{BM}
$$

prompt.text: What is meant by 'disproportionation' of an oxidation state? Give an example.

flow.text: Disproportionation happens when a particular oxidation state becomes less stable than other oxidation states, one lower and one higher. For example, manganese (VI) becomes unstable relative to manganese(VII) and manganese (IV) in acidic solution.

items.topic: Mn2+ vs Fe2+ stability to oxidation

prompt.text: Why are $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$ compounds more stable than $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ towards oxidation to their +3 state?

flow.text:
Electronic configuration of $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$ is $[\mathrm{Ar}]^{18} 3 d^{5}$. Electronic configuration of $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ is $[\mathrm{Ar}]^{18} 3 d^{6}$.

Half-filled and fully-filled orbitals are more stable. So Mn in the (+2) state has a stable $d^{5}$ configuration. This is why $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$ resists oxidation to $\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}$.

$\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ has $3 d^{6}$ configuration. By losing one electron, it changes to a more stable $3 d^{5}$ configuration. So $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ easily gets oxidized to the $\mathrm{Fe}^{+3}$ oxidation state.

prompt.text: Explain briefly how +2 state becomes more and more stable in the first half of the first row transition elements with increasing atomic number?

flow.text: The oxidation states displayed by the first half of the first row of transition metals are given in the table below.

We can see that all the metals except Sc show the +2 oxidation state. Also, moving from Sc to Mn, the atomic number increases from 21 to 25. So the number of electrons in the $3 d$-orbital also increases from 1 to 5.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{Sc}(+2)=d^{1} \\
& \mathrm{Ti}(+2)=d^{2} \\
& \mathrm{~V}(+2)=d^{3} \\
& \mathrm{Cr}(+2)=d^{4} \\
& \mathrm{Mn}(+2)=d^{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

These metals reach the +2 oxidation state by losing two $4 s$ electrons. The number of $d$ electrons in the (+2) state also increases from $\mathrm{Ti}(+2)$ to $\mathrm{Mn}(+2)$, so the stability of the +2 state increases, as the $d$-orbital becomes more and more half-filled. Mn (+2) has $d^{5}$ electrons — a half-filled $d$ shell, which is highly stable.

items.topic: Electronic configuration and oxidation state stability

prompt.text: To what extent do the electronic configurations decide the stability of oxidation states in the first series of the transition elements? Illustrate your answer with examples.

flow.text:
The elements in the first half of the transition series show many oxidation states. Mn shows the maximum number, from +2 to +7. The stability of the +2 oxidation state increases as the atomic number increases, because more electrons are filling the $d$-orbital.

Sc, however, does not show a +2 oxidation state. Its electronic configuration is $4 s^{2} 3 d^{1}$. It loses all three electrons to form $\mathrm{Sc}^{3+}$. The +3 state of Sc is very stable because, by losing all three electrons, it gets the stable noble gas configuration [Ar]. Ti (+4) and V(+5) are very stable for the same reason.

For Mn, the +2 state is very stable because after losing two electrons, its $d$-orbital is exactly half-filled, $[\mathrm{Ar}] 3 d^{5}$.

prompt.text: What is lanthanoid contraction? What are the consequences of lanthanoid contraction?

flow.text:
As we move along the lanthanoid series, the atomic number increases by one each time. So the number of electrons and protons in the atom also increases by one.

Since the new electrons are added to the same shell, the effective nuclear charge increases. This is because the increase in nuclear attraction from the added proton is greater than the increase in repulsion from the added electron.

Also, as the atomic number increases, the number of electrons in the $4 f$ orbital increases too. These $4 f$ electrons shield poorly. So the effective nuclear charge felt by the outer electrons increases, and the nucleus pulls the outermost electrons in more strongly.

This causes a steady decrease in the size of the lanthanoids as the atomic number increases. This is called lanthanoid contraction.

## Consequences of lanthanoid contraction

(i) It explains the similarity in the properties of the second and third transition series.
(ii) It makes it possible to separate the lanthanoids from each other.
(iii) It causes the basic strength of the lanthanide hydroxides to vary. (Basic strength decreases from $\mathrm{La}(\mathrm{OH})_{3}$ to $\mathrm{Lu}(\mathrm{OH})_{3}$.)

prompt.text: What are the characteristics of the transition elements and why are they called transition elements? Which of the $d$-block elements may not be regarded as the transition elements?

flow.text:
Transition elements are elements whose atoms or ions (in a stable oxidation state) have a partially filled $d$-orbital. These elements lie in the $d$-block. Their properties are a transition between the $s$-block and the $p$-block. That is why they are called transition elements.

Zn, Cd, and Hg are not classified as transition elements because they have a completely filled $d$-subshell.

prompt.text: In what way is the electronic configuration of the transition elements different from that of the non transition elements?

flow.text:
Transition metals have a partially filled $d$-orbital. So the electronic configuration of transition elements is $(\mathrm{n}-1) d^{1-10} \mathrm{n} s^{0-2}$.

Non-transition elements either have no $d$-orbital or have a fully filled $d$-orbital. So the electronic configuration of non-transition elements is $\mathrm{ns}^{1-2}$ or $\mathrm{ns}_{2} \mathrm{n} p_{1-6}$.

prompt.text: What are the different oxidation states exhibited by the lanthanoids?

flow.text: In the lanthanide series, +3 oxidation state is most common i.e., $\operatorname{Ln}($ III $)$ compounds are predominant. However, +2 and +4 oxidation states can also be found in the solution or in solid compounds.

prompt.text: Explain giving reasons:
Transition metals and many of their compounds show paramagnetic behaviour.

flow.text: Transition metals show paramagnetic behaviour. Paramagnetism happens because of unpaired electrons — each unpaired electron has a magnetic moment from its spin and orbital angular momentum. But in the first transition series, the orbital angular momentum is quenched. So the paramagnetism we see comes only from the unpaired electrons.

prompt.text: The enthalpies of atomisation of the transition metals are high.

flow.text: Transition elements have a high effective nuclear charge and many valence electrons. So they form very strong metallic bonds. This is why the enthalpy of atomisation of transition metals is high.

prompt.text: The transition metals generally form coloured compounds.

flow.text:
Most complexes of transition metals are coloured. This happens because an electron absorbs radiation from the visible region and jumps from one $d$-orbital to another.

In the presence of ligands, the $d$-orbitals split into two sets with different energies. So electrons can move from one set toanother. This transition needs only a small amount of energy, which falls in the visible region.

The metal ion absorbs radiation of one particular wavelength and reflects the rest. This reflected light gives the solution its colour.

prompt.text: Transition metals and their many compounds act as good catalyst.

flow.text:
The catalytic activity of transition elements can be explained by two facts.
(a) Because they can show variable oxidation states and form complexes, transition metals form unstable intermediate compounds. This gives the reaction a new path with lower activation energy, $E_{\mathrm{a}}$.
(b) Transition metals also give the reaction a suitable surface to occur on.

prompt.text: What are interstitial compounds? Why are such compounds well known for transition metals?

flow.text: Transition metals are large and have many interstitial sites. They can trap small atoms of other elements — such as H, C, and N — in these interstitial sites of their crystal lattice. The compounds formed this way are called interstitial compounds.

prompt.text: How is the variability in oxidation states of transition metals different from that of the non transition metals? Illustrate with examples.

flow.text:
In transition elements, the oxidation state can vary from +1 up to the highest state, formed by removing all the valence electrons. These oxidation states differ from each other by 1 ($\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+} ; \mathrm{Cu}^{+}$and $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$).

In non-transition elements, the oxidation states differ by 2 — for example, +2 and +4 or +3 and +5, etc.

items.topic: Potassium dichromate preparation and pH effect

prompt.text: Describe the preparation of potassium dichromate from iron chromite ore. What is the effect of increasing pH on a solution of potassium dichromate?

flow.text:
Potassium dichromate is prepared from chromite ore $\left(\mathrm{FeCr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}\right)$ in the following steps.
Step (1): Preparation of sodium chromate

$$
4 \mathrm{FeCr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}+16 \mathrm{NaOH}+7 \mathrm{O}_{2} \longrightarrow 8 \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CrO}_{4}+2 \mathrm{Fe}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}+8 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

Step (2): Conversion of sodium chromate into sodium dichromate

$$
2 \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CrO}_{4}+\text { conc. } \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{Cr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{7}+\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

Step(3): Conversion of sodium dichromate to potassium dichromate

$$
\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{Cr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{7}+2 \mathrm{KCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{~K}_{2} \mathrm{Cr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{7}+2 \mathrm{NaCl}
$$

Potassium chloride is less soluble than sodium chloride. So it is obtained as orange coloured crystals, which can be removed by filtration.
The dichromate ion $\left(\mathrm{Cr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{7}^{2-}\right)$ exists in equilibrium with the chromate ion $\left(\mathrm{CrO}_{4}^{2-}\right)_{\text {ion at } \mathrm{pH} 4}$. Changing the pH can convert one into the other.

$$
2 \mathrm{CrO}_{4}^{2-} \hat{ \pm}_{\text {Alkali }}^{2 \text { alaid }} 2 \mathrm{HCrO}_{4}^{-} \quad \hat{ \pm}_{\text {Alkalt }}^{\text {2ladat }} \mathrm{Cr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{7}^{2-}
$$

prompt.text: Describe the preparation of potassium permanganate. How does the acidified permanganate solution react with (i) iron(II) ions (ii) $\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ and (iii) oxalic acid? Write the ionic equations for the reactions.

flow.text: Acidified $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution oxidizes Fe (II) ions to Fe (III) ions i.e., ferrous ions to ferric ions.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+8 \mathrm{H}^{+}+5 \mathrm{e}^{-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \\
& \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\left.\longrightarrow \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+\mathrm{e}^{-}\right] \times 5 \\

& \hline
\end{aligned}
$$
Acidified potassium permanganate oxidizes $\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ to sulphuric acid.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+6 \mathrm{H}^{+}+5 \mathrm{e}^{-}\left.\longrightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+3 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right] \times 2 \\
& 2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}+2 \mathrm{SO}_{2}+\mathrm{O}_{2}\left.\longrightarrow 4 \mathrm{H}^{+}+2 \mathrm{SO}_{4}^{2-}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-}\right] \times 5 \\

& \hline
\end{aligned}
$$
Acidified potassium permanganate oxidizes oxalic acid to carbon dioxide.

$$
\begin{aligned}

& \mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}^{2-}\left.\longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{CO}_{2}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-}\right] \times 5 \\
& \hline 2 \mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+5 \mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}^{2-}+16 \mathrm{H}^{+} \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+10 \mathrm{CO}_{2}+8 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \\

items.topic: E-degree values and metal ion stability

prompt.text: the stability of $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ in acid solution as compared to that of $\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}$ or $\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}$ and

flow.text: The ${ }^{\ominus}$ value for $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+} / \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ is higher than that for $\mathrm{Cr}^{3+} / \mathrm{Cr}^{2+}$ and lower than that for $\mathrm{Mn}^{3+} / \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$. So, the reduction of $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ to $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ is easier than the reduction of $\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}$ to $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$, but not as easy as the reduction of $\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}$ to $\mathrm{Cr}^{2+}$. Hence, $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ is more stable than $\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}$, but less stable than $\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}$. These metal ions can be arranged in the increasing order of their stability as: $\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}<\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}<\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}$

prompt.text: the ease with which iron can be oxidised as compared to a similar process for either chromium or manganese metal.

flow.text:
The reduction potentials for the given pairs increase in the following order.
$\mathrm{Mn}^{2+} / \mathrm{Mn}<\mathrm{Cr}^{2+} / \mathrm{Cr}<\mathrm{Fe}^{2+} / \mathrm{Fe}$

So, the oxidation of Fe to $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ is not as easy as the oxidation of Cr to $\mathrm{Cr}^{2+}$ and the oxidation of Mn to $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$. Thus, these metals can be arranged in the increasing order of their ability to get oxidised as: $\mathrm{Fe}<\mathrm{Cr}<\mathrm{Mn}$

prompt.text: Compare the stability of +2 oxidation state for the elements of the first transition series.

flow.text: From the table, we can see that Mn shows the maximum number of oxidation states, varying from +2 to +7. The number of oxidation states increases from Sc to Mn, then decreases from Mn to Zn, because the number of available unpaired electrons decreases. The +2 oxidation state becomes more stable moving from top to bottom. This is because it becomes harder and harder to remove the third electron from the $d$-orbital as we move from top to bottom.

prompt.text: Compare the chemistry of actinoids with that of the lanthanoids with special reference to:
electronic configuration

flow.text: The general electronic configuration is $[\mathrm{Xe}]^{54} 4 f^{0-14} 5 d^{0-1} 6 s^{2}$ for lanthanoids and $[\mathrm{Rn}]^{86} 5 f^{1-14} 6 d^{0-1} 7 s^{2}$ for actinoids. Unlike $4 f$ orbitals, the $5 f$ orbitals are not buried as deeply, so they take part in bonding more.

prompt.text: atomic and ionic sizes and

flow.text: Like lanthanoids, actinoids also show actinoid contraction — an overall decrease in atomic and ionic radii. This contraction is greater, because of the poor shielding effect of the $5 f$ orbitals.

prompt.text: oxidation state

flow.text:
The main oxidation state of lanthanoids is +3. We also sometimes see +2 and +4, because of the extra stability of fully-filled and half-filled orbitals.

Actinoids show a wider range of oxidation states, because the $5 f, 6 d$ and $7 s$ levels have comparable energies. But +3 is still the main oxidation state for actinoids too. Like lanthanoids, actinoids form more compounds in the +3 state than in the +4 state.

prompt.text: chemical reactivity.

flow.text:
In the lanthanide series, the earlier members are more reactive — their reactivity is comparable to Ca. As the atomic number increases, the lanthanides start behaving more like Al.

Actinoids, on the other hand, are highly reactive metals, especially when finely divided. Added to boiling water, they give a mixture of oxide and hydride. They combine with most non-metals at moderate temperatures. Alkalies have no effect on them. Among acids, only nitric acid affects them slightly, because it forms a protective oxide layer.

items.topic: Reasons for transition metal ion behaviour

prompt.text: How would you account for the following:
Of the $d^{4}$ species, $\mathrm{Cr}^{2+}$ is strongly reducing while manganese(III) is strongly oxidising.

flow.text:
$\mathrm{Cr}^{2+}$ is strongly reducing. It has a $d^{4}$ configuration. As a reducing agent, it gets oxidised to $\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}$ (electronic configuration $d^{3}$). This $d^{3}$ configuration can also be written as $t_{2 g}^{3}$ configuration, which is more stable.

$\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}\left(d^{4}\right)$, on the other hand, acts as an oxidizing agent and gets reduced to $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\left(d^{5}\right)$. This has an exactly half-filled $d$-orbital, so it is highly stable.

prompt.text: Cobalt(II) is stable in aqueous solution but in the presence of complexing reagents it is easily oxidised.

flow.text: $\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{II})$ is stable in aqueous solution. But in the presence of strong field complexing reagents, it is oxidised to Co (III). The $3^{\text {rd }}$ ionization energy for Co is high. However, the larger crystal field stabilization energy (CFSE) released by strong field ligands is enough to overcome this ionization energy.

prompt.text: The $d^{1}$ configuration is very unstable in ions.

flow.text: Ions with a $d^{1}$ configuration tend to lose one more electron to reach the stable $d^{0}$ configuration. Also, the hydration or lattice energy is more than enough to remove the one electron present in the $d$-orbital of these ions. So they act as reducing agents.

prompt.text: What is meant by 'disproportionation'? Give two examples of disproportionation reaction in aqueous solution.

flow.text:
Sometimes a relatively less stable oxidation state undergoes a reaction in which it is oxidised and reduced at the same time. This is called disproportionation.

For example,
Here, Cr(V) is oxidized to Cr(VI) and reduced to Cr(III).
Here, $\mathrm{Mn}(\mathrm{VI})$ is oxidized to Mn (VII) and reduced to Mn (IV).

prompt.text: Which metal in the first series of transition metals exhibits +1 oxidation state most frequently and why?

flow.text: In the first transition series, Cu very often shows the +1 oxidation state. This is because $\mathrm{Cu}(+1)$ has an electronic configuration of $[\mathrm{Ar}] 3 d^{10}$. Its completely filled $d$-orbital makes it highly stable.

prompt.text: Calculate the number of unpaired electrons in the following gaseous ions: $\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}$, $\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}, \mathrm{V}^{3+}$ and $\mathrm{Ti}^{3+}$. Which one of these is the most stable in aqueous solution?

items.topic: Transition metal oxide and oxoanion trends

prompt.text: Give examples and suggest reasons for the following features of the transition metal chemistry:
The lowest oxide of transition metal is basic, the highest is amphoteric/acidic.

flow.text:
In a lower oxide of a transition metal, the metal atom has a low oxidation state. So some of its valence electrons are not used in bonding, and it can donate electrons — behaving as a base.

In a higher oxide, the metal atom has a high oxidation state. Here the valence electrons are used up in bonding, so they are unavailable, and the effective nuclear charge is also high. So it can accept electrons — behaving as an acid.

For example, $\mathrm{Mn}^{\mathrm{II}} \mathrm{O}$ is basic and $\mathrm{Mn}_{2}^{\mathrm{VII}} \mathrm{O}_{7}$ is acidic.

prompt.text: A transition metal exhibits highest oxidation state in oxides and fluorides.

flow.text: Oxygen and fluorine are strong oxidising agents, because they are highly electronegative and small in size. So they bring out the highest oxidation states in transition metals — which is why a transition metal shows its highest oxidation states in oxides and fluorides. For example, in $\mathrm{OsF}_{6}$ and $\mathrm{V}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{5}$, the oxidation states of Os and V are +6 and +5 respectively.

prompt.text: The highest oxidation state is exhibited in oxoanions of a metal.

flow.text:
Oxygen is a strong oxidising agent because of its high electronegativity and small size.

So, oxo-anions of a metal have the highest oxidation state. For example, in $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$, the oxidation state of Mn is +7.

prompt.text: Indicate the steps in the preparation of:
$\mathrm{K}_{2} \mathrm{Cr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{7}$ from chromite ore.

flow.text:
Potassium dichromate $\left(\mathrm{K}_{2} \mathrm{Cr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{7}\right)$ is prepared from chromite ore $\left(\mathrm{FeCr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}\right)$ in the following steps.

Step (1): Preparation of sodium chromate

$$
4 \mathrm{FeCr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}+16 \mathrm{NaOH}+7 \mathrm{O}_{2} \longrightarrow 8 \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CrO}_{4}+2 \mathrm{Fe}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}+8 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

Step (2): Conversion of sodium chromate into sodium dichromate

$$
2 \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CrO}_{4}+\text { conc. } \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{Cr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{7}+\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

Step(3): Conversion of sodium dichromate to potassium dichromate

$$
\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{Cr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{7}+2 \mathrm{KCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{~K}_{2} \mathrm{Cr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{7}+2 \mathrm{NaCl}
$$

Potassium chloride is less soluble than sodium chloride. So it is obtained as orange coloured crystals, which can be removed by filtration.
The dichromate ion $\left(\mathrm{Cr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{7}^{2-}\right)$ exists in equilibrium with the chromate ion $\left(\mathrm{CrO}_{4}^{2-}\right)_{\text {ion at } \mathrm{pH} 4}$. Changing the pH can convert one into the other.

$$
\begin{array}{llcl}
2 \mathrm{CrO}_{4}^{2-} & \stackrel{\text { Acid }}{\text { Alkali }} & 2 \mathrm{HCrO}_{4}^{-} & \stackrel{\text { Acid }}{\leftrightarrow} \\
\text { Chromate } & & \text { Hydrogen } & \\
\text { (Yellow) } & & \text { chromate } & \\
\text { (Yellow } & & \text { Dichromate } \\
\text { (Orange) } &
\end{array}
$$

prompt.text: $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ from pyrolusite ore.
What are alloys? Name an important alloy which contains some of the lanthanoid metals. Mention its uses.

flow.text:
An alloy is a solid solution of two or more elements in a metallic matrix. It can be either a partial solid solution or a complete solid solution. Alloys usually have different physical properties from those of the component elements.

An important lanthanoid alloy is Mischmetal. It contains lanthanoids (94-95\%), iron (5\%), and traces of S, C, Si, Ca, and Al.

Uses

(1) Mischmetal is used in cigarettes and gas lighters.
(2) It is used in flame throwing tanks.
(3) It is used in tracer bullets and shells.

prompt.text: What are inner transition elements? Decide which of the following atomic numbers are the atomic numbers of the inner transition elements : 29, 59, 74, 95, 102, 104.

flow.text: Inner transition metals are elements whose last electron enters the $f$-orbital. Elements in which the $4 f$ and the $5 f$ orbitals are progressively filled are called $f$-block elements. Among the given atomic numbers, 59, 95, and 102 belong to the inner transition elements.

prompt.text: The chemistry of the actinoid elements is not so smooth as that of the lanthanoids. Justify this statement by giving some examples from the oxidation state of these elements.

flow.text:
Lanthanoids mainly show three oxidation states (+2, +3, +4). Of these, +3 is the most common. Lanthanoids show only a limited number of oxidation states because the energy difference between the $4 f, 5 d$ and $6 s$ orbitals is quite large.

The energy difference between the $5 f, 6 d$ and $7 s$ orbitals, on the other hand, is very small. So actinoids show a large number of oxidation states. For example, uranium and plutonium show +3, +4, +5, and +6 oxidation states, while neptunium shows +3, +4, +5, and +7. The most common oxidation state for actinoids is also +3.

prompt.text: Which is the last element in the series of the actinoids? Write the electronic configuration of this element. Comment on the possible oxidation state of this element.

flow.text: The last element in the actinoid series is lawrencium, Lr. Its atomic number is 103, and its electronic configuration is $[\mathrm{Rn}] 5 f^{14} 6 d^{1} 7 s^{2}$. Its most common oxidation state is +3, because losing 3 electrons gives it the stable $f^{14}$ configuration.

flow.text: The lanthanides that show +2 and +4 states are listed in the table below. The atomic numbers of the elements are given in parentheses.

prompt.text: Compare the chemistry of the actinoids with that of lanthanoids with reference to: (i) electronic configuration (ii) oxidation states and (iii) chemical reactivity.

flow.text:
## Electronic configuration

The general electronic configuration is $[\mathrm{Xe}]^{54} 4 f^{0-14} 5 d^{0-1} 6 s^{2}$ for lanthanoids and $[\mathrm{Rn}]^{86} 5 f^{1-14} 6 d^{0-1} 7 s^{2}$ for actinoids. Unlike $4 f$ orbitals, the $5 f$ orbitals are not buried as deeply, so they take part in bonding more.

## Oxidation states

The main oxidation state of lanthanoids is +3. We also sometimes see +2 and +4 oxidation states, because of the extra stability of fully-filled and half-filled orbitals. Actinoids show a wider range of oxidation states, because the $5 f, 6 d$ and $7 s$ levels have comparable energies. But +3 is still the main oxidation state for actinoids too. Like lanthanoids, actinoids form more compounds in the +3 state than in the +4 state.

## Chemical reactivity

In the lanthanide series, the earlier members are more reactive — their reactivity is comparable to Ca. As the atomic number increases, the lanthanides start behaving more like Al.

Actinoids, on the other hand, are highly reactive metals, especially when finely divided. Added to boiling water, they give a mixture of oxide and hydride. They combine with most non-metals at moderate temperatures. Alkalies have no effect on them. Among acids, only nitric acid affects them slightly, because it forms a protective oxide layer.

items.topic: First series vs heavier transition series

prompt.text:
Compare the general characteristics of the first series of the transition metals with those of the second and third series metals in the respective vertical columns. Give special emphasis on the following points:
    (i) electronic configurations (ii) oxidation states (iii) ionisation enthalpies and (iv) atomic sizes.

flow.text:
In each of the three transition series, the number of oxidation states shown by the elements is highest in the middle and lowest at the two ends.

However, +2 and +3 oxidation states are quite stable for all elements in the first transition series — all its metals form stable compounds in the +2 and +3 oxidation states. The stability of the +2 and +3 oxidation states decreases in the second and third transition series, where higher oxidation states matter more instead.
For example, $\left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{Cn})_{6}\right]^{4-},\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{6}\right]^{3+},\left[\mathrm{Ti}\left(\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)_{6}\right]^{3+}$ are stable complexes, but no such complexes are known for second- and third-series metals such as Mo, W, Rh, In. They instead form complexes with high oxidation states. For example: $\mathrm{WCl}_{6}, \mathrm{ReF}_{7}$, $\mathrm{RuO}_{4}$, etc.

In each of the three transition series, the first ionisation enthalpy increases from left to right, though there are some exceptions. The first ionisation enthalpies of the third transition series are higher than those of the first and second transition series. This is because of the poor shielding effect of $4 f$ electrons in the third transition series.

Certain elements in the second transition series have higher first ionisation enthalpies than the elements in the same vertical column of the first transition series. There are also elements in the $2^{\text {nd }}$ transition series whose first ionisation enthalpies are lower than those of the elements in the same vertical column of the $1^{\text {st }}$ transition series.

Atomic size generally decreases from left to right across a period. Among the three transition series, the atomic sizes of the elements in the second transition series are greater than those of the elements in the same vertical column of the first transition series. However, the atomic sizes of the elements in the third transition series are virtually the same as those of the corresponding members in the second transition series. This is due to lanthanoid contraction.

prompt.text: Write down the number of 3d electrons in each of the following ions: $\mathrm{Ti}^{2+}, \mathrm{V}^{2+}$, $\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}, \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}, \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}, \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}, \mathrm{Co}^{2+}, \mathrm{Ni}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$. Indicate how would you expect the five 3d orbitals to be occupied for these hydrated ions (octahedral).
Comment on the statement that elements of the first transition series possess many properties different from those of heavier transition elements.

flow.text:
The properties of the elements of the first transition series differ from those of the heavier transition elements in many ways.

(i) The atomic sizes of the elements of the first transition series are smaller than those of the heavier elements (elements of the $2^{\text {nd }}$ and $3^{\text {rd }}$ transition series). However, the atomic sizes of the elements in the third transition series are virtually the same as those of the corresponding members in the second transition series. This is due to lanthanoid contraction.

(ii) +2 and +3 oxidation states are more common for elements in the first transition series, while higher oxidation states are more common for the heavier elements.

(iii) The enthalpies of atomisation of the elements in the first transition series are lower than those of the corresponding elements in the second and third transition series.

(iv) The melting and boiling points of the first transition series are lower than those of the heavier transition elements. This is because of stronger metallic bonding (M-M bonding).

(v) The elements of the first transition series form low-spin or high-spin complexes depending upon the strength of the ligand field. However, the heavier transition elements form only low-spin complexes, irrespective of the strength of the ligand field.

prompt.text: Silver atom has completely filled $d$ orbitals ( $4 d^{10}$ ) in its ground state. How can you say that it is a transition element?

flow.text: Ag has a completely filled $4 d$ orbital ( $4 d^{10} 5 s^{1}$ ) in its ground state. Silver shows two oxidation states, +1 and +2. In the +1 state, one electron is removed from the $s$-orbital. In the +2 state, an electron is removed from the $d$-orbital. This makes the $d$-orbital incomplete ( $4 d^{9}$ ). So, silver is a transition element.

prompt.text: In the series $\mathrm{Sc}(Z=21)$ to $\mathrm{Zn}(Z=30)$, the enthalpy of atomisation of zinc is the lowest, i.e., $126 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. Why?

flow.text: The enthalpy of atomization depends on how strong the metallic bonding is. The stronger the metallic bonding, the higher the enthalpy of atomization. All transition metals, except Zn (electronic configuration: $3 d^{10} 4 s^{2}$ ), have some unpaired electrons. These unpaired electrons give stronger metallic bonding. Zn has no such unpaired electrons, so its inter-atomic bonding is the weakest. This is why Zn has the lowest enthalpy of atomization.

items.topic: Number of oxidation states in 3d series

prompt.text: Which of the $3 d$ series of the transition metals exhibits the largest number of oxidation states and why?

flow.text: Mn has the maximum number of unpaired electrons present in the $d$-subshell (5 electrons). Hence, Mn exhibits the largest number of oxidation states, ranging from +2 to +7.

prompt.text: The $E^{\circ}\left(\mathrm{M}^{2+} / \mathrm{M}\right)$ value for copper is positive (+0.34V). What is possible reason for this? (Hint: consider its high $\Delta_{\mathrm{a}} H^{\mathrm{o}}$ and low $\Delta_{\text {hyd }} H^{\mathrm{o}}$ )

flow.text:
The $E^{\theta}\left(\mathrm{M}^{2+} / \mathrm{M}\right)$ value of a metal depends on the energy changes involved in the following:

1. Sublimation: The energy required for converting one mole of an atom from the solid state to the gaseous state.
2. Ionization: The energy required to take out electrons from one mole of atoms in the gaseous state.
3. Hydration: The energy released when one mole of ions are hydrated.

$$
\mathrm{M}_{(g)}^{2+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{M}_{(a q)}^{2+} \quad \Delta_{\text {hyd }} H(\text { Hydration energy })
$$
Copper has a high energy of atomization and low hydration energy. So, the $E^{\ominus}\left(\mathrm{M}^{2+} / \mathrm{M}\right)$ value for copper is positive.

prompt.text: How would you account for the irregular variation of ionisation enthalpies (first and second) in the first series of the transition elements?

flow.text:
Ionization enthalpies increase across the series because the inner $d$-orbitals keep filling up. Some configurations, such as $d^{0}, d^{5}, d^{10}$, are extra stable. Elements with these configurations have very high ionization enthalpies.

For the first ionization energy, Cr has a low value. This is because after losing one electron, Cr reaches the stable configuration $\left(3 d^{5}\right)$. Zn, on the other hand, has an exceptionally high first ionization energy, because an electron has to be removed from its stable, fully-filled orbitals $\left(3 d^{10} 4 s^{2}\right)$.

Second ionization energies are higher than first ionization energies, since it is harder to remove an electron once one electron is already gone. Cr and Cu also have exceptionally high second ionization energies, because after losing the first electron, they reach the stable configurations $\left(\mathrm{Cr}^{+}: 3 d^{5}\right.$ and $\left.\mathrm{Cu}^{+}: 3 d^{10}\right)$. Removing one more electron from this stable configuration needs a lot of energy.

prompt.text: Why is the highest oxidation state of a metal exhibited in its oxide or fluoride only?

flow.text: Both oxide and fluoride ions are highly electronegative and have a very small size. Due to these properties, they are able to oxidize the metal to its highest oxidation state.

items.topic: Stability of Cu+ in aqueous solution

prompt.text: Explain why $\mathrm{Cu}^{+}$ion is not stable in aqueous solutions?

flow.text: In an aqueous medium, $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ is more stable than $\mathrm{Cu}^{+}$. Energy is needed to remove one electron from $\mathrm{Cu}^{+}$ to $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$, but the high hydration energy of $\mathrm{Cu} 2+$ makes up for it. So, $\mathrm{Cu}^{+}$ion is unstable in aqueous solution. It disproportionates to give $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ and Cu.

prompt.text: Actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than lanthanoid contraction. Why?

flow.text: In actinoids, $5 f$ orbitals are filled. These $5 f$ orbitals have a poorer shielding effect than $4 f$ orbitals (in lanthanoids). So, the effective nuclear charge on valence-shell electrons is much higher in actinoids than in lanthanoids. This is why the size contraction is greater in actinoids than in lanthanoids.
